## Big Question {.role-slide}

What must a design do before a model can estimate the intended linguistic comparison?

## Data {.role-slide}

An experiment compares recognition after familiar and unfamiliar accent training.

Each participant completes 40 trials.

## Surprising Fact {.role-slide}

Twenty four participants produce 960 rows, but training was assigned only 24 times.

## Challenge {.role-slide}

A model cannot create condition assignments, item balance, or retained observations that the design did not produce.

## This Module {.role-slide .compact}

1. Identify the unit and mechanism of assignment.
2. Choose a participant structure that preserves the manipulation.
3. Distribute item versions across participants.
4. Declare exclusions and evaluate the complete procedure by simulation.

## Idea {.role-slide}

Winter begins with repeated linguistic observations and asks which observations may count as independent evidence.

<span class="source">Winter 2020, Sections 14.2 and 14.3</span>

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf
:::

## Units of assignment {.section-slide}

What can independently receive a condition?

## Question {.role-slide}

Does accent training vary across participants or across recognition trials?

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [**unit of assignment**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics) is the entity that can independently receive a condition.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics
:::

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [**unit of observation**](https://bookdown.org/pkaldunn/Book/UnitsObsAnalysis.html) is the entity represented by one measured response.

Recall the [unit of analysis](../../foundations/linguistic-data.html).

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://bookdown.org/pkaldunn/Book/UnitsObsAnalysis.html
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

Ask what could have received a different condition under the actual procedure.

## Output {.role-slide}

Twelve trial rows from four participants contain twelve observations and four assignment units.

## Question {.role-slide}

A classroom receives one teaching method. Each student gives five responses.

What is assigned, and what is observed?

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Additional trials may improve measurement. They do not add independent condition assignments.

## Random assignment {.section-slide}

How conditions reach assignment units

## Challenge {.role-slide}

If participants choose the accent condition, prior accent experience may differ between conditions.

## Answer {.role-slide}

The [**assignment mechanism**](https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics) is the probability rule that selects a condition for each assignment unit.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

Under independent assignment with equal probabilities,

$$
P(Z_i=1)=P(Z_i=0)=.5.
$$

## Surprising Fact {.role-slide}

A valid mechanism can produce a realized split of three participants and five participants.

Balance is an expectation, not a guarantee for one sample.

## Approach {.role-slide}

Restricted random assignment samples only from assignments that satisfy a declared balance condition.

## Important Point #1 {.role-slide}

Random sampling concerns entry into the study.

Random assignment concerns allocation of conditions within the study.

## Important Point #2 {.role-slide}

Save the realized assignment table and conceal future assignments from recruiters.

## Within-participant designs {.section-slide}

Each participant supplies a contrast

## Data {.role-slide}

Participants differ in their use of a seven point acceptability scale.

Stable response habits may obscure a construction contrast.

## Answer {.role-slide}

In a [**within-participant design**](https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/), each participant contributes observations to more than one condition.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

Each participant supplies a difference.

$$
D_i=Y_{i1}-Y_{i0},\qquad \bar D=\frac{1}{n}\sum_iD_i
$$

Recall [paired observations](../../statistical-inference/paired-observations.html).

## Output {.role-slide}

Four active minus passive differences are $1$, $2$, $1$, and $0$.

Their mean is one scale point.

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**carryover effect**](https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/) occurs when an earlier condition changes a later response.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## Question {.role-slide}

If every active sentence precedes its passive counterpart, what two explanations are combined in the condition difference?

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Stable participant shifts may cancel, but order and lasting effects remain part of the design.

## Between-participant designs {.section-slide}

Comparing groups

## Data {.role-slide}

Accent training changes a listener. The original untrained state cannot be restored.

## Answer {.role-slide}

In a [**between-participant design**](https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/), each participant contributes observations to only one condition.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

The comparison is between group means.

$$
\widehat\Delta=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0
$$

Recall [independent means](../../statistical-inference/independent-means.html).

## Output {.role-slide}

Familiar training mean: $.800$

Unfamiliar training mean: $.715$

Estimated difference: $.085$

## Challenge {.role-slide}

Sorting two group vectors and pairing their rows invents a relation that the design never created.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Use a between-participant design when the manipulation cannot be repeated without changing its meaning.

## Counterbalancing {.section-slide}

Distributing item versions

## Question {.role-slide}

How can each item appear in every condition without showing every participant every version?

## Answer {.role-slide}

[**Counterbalancing**](https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/) distributes item versions across lists so that condition is not tied to item identity.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## Method {.role-slide}

| item | list 1 | list 2 |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A | condition 1 | condition 2 |
| B | condition 2 | condition 1 |

## Important Point #1 {.role-slide}

The list map must be assigned to participants by a recorded procedure.

A balanced file does not show that lists reached participants appropriately.

## Important Point #2 {.role-slide}

Counterbalancing distributes condition versions. It does not make responses from the same participant or item independent.

## Question {.role-slide}

After exclusions, condition 1 has fewer observations for one item.

Is the collected dataset still balanced?

## Exclusion rules {.section-slide}

Defining the analyzed set

## Data {.role-slide}

A microphone failure and a 4,000 millisecond response both look unusual.

Only one is necessarily a missing measurement.

## Approach {.role-slide}

Let $R_i=1$ when observation $i$ is retained and $R_i=0$ when it is excluded.

The retained analysis conditions on $R_i=1$.

## Data {.role-slide}

All five grammatical trials return responses.

Two of five ungrammatical trials time out.

## Result #1 {.role-slide}

Among retained trials, the mean difference is only 10 milliseconds.

## Result #2 {.role-slide}

The timeout rate is zero in one condition and forty percent in the other.

## Interpretation {.role-slide}

The retained mean describes trials that produced a response before timeout.

It does not show that the manipulation had little effect.

## Method {.role-slide .compact}

Define rules before inspecting the desired contrast. Report participant and trial flow, reasons for removal, and exclusions by every relevant condition and group.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Exclusion helps define the estimand. It is not merely table cleaning.

## Power by simulation {.section-slide}

Evaluating the complete planned procedure

## Question {.role-slide}

How many participants are needed for a within-participant acceptability experiment?

## Challenge {.role-slide}

There is no answer until we specify a data-generating process and a decision rule.

## Data {.role-slide}

For participant differences,

$$
D_i\sim\operatorname{Normal}(\delta,\sigma_D).
$$

## Method {.role-slide .compact}

1. Generate the exact planned design.
2. Apply the planned exclusions.
3. Fit the planned analysis.
4. Apply the planned decision rule.
5. Repeat the complete procedure.

## Output {.role-slide}

Estimated power is the proportion of simulated studies that meet the decision rule under the stated generating process.

## Answer {.role-slide}

A [**power curve**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=187) shows estimated power across participant counts or effect assumptions.

::: {.notes}
[Sources]

https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=187
:::

## Challenge {.role-slide}

Increasing the number of simulations reduces simulation error. It does not add participants to the planned study.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

Power is conditional on the assumed process, complete design, analysis, and decision rule.

## Conclusion {.section-slide}

Design before analysis

## Big Question {.role-slide}

What must a design do before a model can estimate the intended linguistic comparison?

## Answer {.role-slide .compact}

1. Count assignments at the level where conditions can vary.
2. Match participant structure to the manipulation.
3. Counterbalance item versions and record list assignment.
4. Treat retention as part of the estimand.
5. Simulate the complete planned procedure.

## Upshot {.role-slide}

A statistical model begins after the design has already determined which comparisons the data can support.
